igcse-0580-equations-model.description: Turn a relationship into symbols, use the equality and explain what the answer counts.

sections.title: When should I write an equals sign?
sections.label: Equal
sections.intro: An expression describes an amount. An equation says two amounts have the same value. Find the two amounts in the story.

blocks.html: Name the unknown, write the two amounts, then put an equals sign between them.

figure.alt: Two level platforms of a balance with equal loads.
figure.caption: If the amounts are equal, applying the same change to both sides keeps them equal.

blocks.prompt: A craft class charges £4 to join and £5 for each session. Tari pays £39 for \(x\) sessions. Write an equation in \(x\).
blocks.hint: Use an equality between the cost rule and the amount paid.
blocks.solution:
The session charge is \(5x\). Add the joining charge once.

The cost \(4+5x\) must equal \(39\).

The answer is \(4+5x=39\).

blocks.html: Give the fixed charge its own term if it is paid once.

blocks.prompt: A craft class charges £7 to join and £8 for each session. Tari pays £31 for \(x\) sessions. Write an equation in \(x\).
blocks.hint: Use an equality between the cost rule and the amount paid.
blocks.solution:
The session charge is \(8x\). Add the joining charge once.

The cost \(7+8x\) must equal \(31\).

The answer is \(7+8x=31\).

sections.title: How can an equation find a count?
sections.label: Choose
sections.intro: Use one letter for the unknown count and write down what each term measures. Then use inverse operations to isolate the count.

blocks.html: Write the result with the units or a word that tells what the number counts.

blocks.prompt: A robot already has 5 recorded trips. It records 6 more trips each hour until it has 53. After how many hours does it reach that total?
blocks.hint: Subtract the starting count before dividing by the hourly increase.
blocks.solution:
Let \(x\) be the number of hours. The total gives \(5+6x=53\).

Subtract 5 and divide by 6.

The answer is \(8\).

blocks.html: Check the answer in the original situation, including its units.

blocks.prompt: A robot already has 8 recorded trips. It records 9 more trips each hour until it has 44. After how many hours does it reach that total?
blocks.hint: Subtract the starting count before dividing by the hourly increase.
blocks.solution:
Let \(x\) be the number of hours. The total gives \(8+9x=44\).

Subtract 8 and divide by 9.

The answer is \(4\).

sections.title: How can I write a rule for changing totals?
sections.label: Rule
sections.intro: Use letters for both the input and the total. Work out which terms repeat for each new group.

blocks.html: Write a formula that works for every allowed value of the input.

blocks.prompt: A rowing club puts 8 rowers in every boat. It also has 6 coaches. Write a formula for the total number \(t\) of people when it uses \(n\) boats.
blocks.hint: Use a separate term for the people who are not counted per boat.
blocks.solution:
The boats hold \(8n\) rowers altogether.

Add \(6\) coaches to that count.

The answer is \(t=8n+6\).

blocks.html: A fixed part is counted once, however many groups there are.

blocks.prompt: A rowing club puts 11 rowers in every boat. It also has 9 coaches. Write a formula for the total number \(t\) of people when it uses \(n\) boats.
blocks.hint: Use a separate term for the people who are not counted per boat.
blocks.solution:
The boats hold \(11n\) rowers altogether.

Add \(9\) coaches to that count.

The answer is \(t=11n+9\).

sections.title: Which operation should I undo first?
sections.label: Reverse
sections.intro: Solve by leaving the x term alone, then finding the value of one x.

blocks.html: Apply each inverse operation to both sides.

figure.alt: Two operations shown in reverse order, with arrows from right to left.
figure.caption: Start from the given result and work back through the operations.

blocks.hint: Perform the same operation on both sides so the equality stays true.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(15\) from both sides, so \(7x=21\).

Divide both sides by \(7\).

The answer is \(3\).

blocks.html: Subtracting on the left requires subtracting the same amount on the right.

blocks.hint: Perform the same operation on both sides so the equality stays true.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(5\) from both sides, so \(3x=18\).

Divide both sides by \(3\).

The answer is \(6\).

sections.title: What if x is on both sides?
sections.label: Sides
sections.intro: Remove the smaller x term from each side to keep one positive coefficient. You can also solve with a negative coefficient if you keep its sign.

blocks.html: Combine the x terms on one side and the constants on the other.

blocks.hint: Perform the same operation on both sides so the equality stays true.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(4x\) from both sides. This leaves \(8x+16=48\).

Subtract 16 and divide by 8.

The answer is \(4\).

blocks.html: The sign changes only because you have added or subtracted a term on both sides.

blocks.hint: Perform the same operation on both sides so the equality stays true.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(2x\) from both sides. This leaves \(4x+6=34\).

Subtract 6 and divide by 4.

The answer is \(7\).

sections.title: What if x is inside a bracket?
sections.label: Brackets
sections.intro: You can treat an intact bracket as a single quantity, or expand it carefully. Look for an inverse operation that keeps the steps short.

blocks.html: When isolating an intact bracket, remove the outside operations before changing what is inside.

blocks.hint: Perform the same operation on both sides so the equality stays true.
blocks.solution:
Add \(4\) to each side to leave \(9(x+5)=90\).

Divide both sides by 9. Then take 5 away from each side.

The answer is \(5\).

blocks.html: When expanding instead, multiply every term inside the bracket.

blocks.hint: Perform the same operation on both sides so the equality stays true.
blocks.solution:
Add \(7\) to each side to leave \(5(x+3)=55\).

Divide both sides by 5. Then take 3 away from each side.

The answer is \(8\).

igcse-0580-equations-formulae.description: Make one letter the subject using inverse operations where the subject appears once.

sections.title: What does the subject mean?
sections.label: Once
sections.intro: The subject is the letter isolated on one side. Changing the subject expresses the same relationship in a different order.

blocks.html: Undo the last operation used on the new subject, then undo earlier operations.

figure.alt: Two operations shown in reverse order, with arrows from right to left.
figure.caption: Start from the given result and work back through the operations.

blocks.prompt: Make \(x\) the subject of \(p=7x+2\).
blocks.hint: Work backwards through the operations that produce p.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(2\) from both sides, giving \(p-2=7x\).

Divide both sides by \(7\) and write the formula with \(x\) alone on the left.

The answer is \(x=\frac{p-2}{7}\).

blocks.html: Keep the terms grouped with a bracket or a fraction bar.

blocks.prompt: Make \(x\) the subject of \(p=3x+5\).
blocks.hint: Work backwards through the operations that produce p.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(5\) from both sides, giving \(p-5=3x\).

Divide both sides by \(3\) and write the formula with \(x\) alone on the left.

The answer is \(x=\frac{p-5}{3}\).

sections.title: How can I remove a denominator?
sections.label: Denominator
sections.intro: Multiply both sides by the denominator. Then continue to undo operations until the intended letter is alone.

blocks.html: When an entire expression is divided, multiply the entire other side by the denominator.

blocks.prompt: Make \(x\) the subject of \(p=\frac{8x}{3}\).
blocks.hint: Work backwards through the operations that produce p.
blocks.solution:
Multiply both sides by \(3\) to remove the denominator.

Divide both sides by \(8\) and write the formula with \(x\) alone on the left.

The answer is \(x=\frac{3p}{8}\).

blocks.html: A division by a constant can be undone by multiplying by that constant.

blocks.prompt: Make \(x\) the subject of \(p=\frac{4x}{6}\).
blocks.hint: Work backwards through the operations that produce p.
blocks.solution:
Multiply both sides by \(6\) to remove the denominator.

Divide both sides by \(4\) and write the formula with \(x\) alone on the left.

The answer is \(x=\frac{6p}{4}\).

sections.title: How can I check the new rule?
sections.label: Check
sections.intro: Choose simple numbers to check one example in both versions. The formula should reproduce the same relationship.

blocks.html: Read the output as a rule in the remaining letter.

blocks.prompt: The value of \(q\) is given by \(q=10+4a\). Write a formula giving \(a\) in terms of \(q\).
blocks.hint: First undo the added number.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(10\) from each side before dividing.

Divide the resulting expression by \(4\).

The answer is \(a=\frac{q-10}{4}\).

blocks.html: A quick numerical check can reveal a sign error. Keep the rearrangement as your mathematical justification.

blocks.prompt: The value of \(q\) is given by \(q=6+7a\). Write a formula giving \(a\) in terms of \(q\).
blocks.hint: First undo the added number.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(6\) from each side before dividing.

Divide the resulting expression by \(7\).

The answer is \(a=\frac{q-6}{7}\).

igcse-0580-equations-linear-simultaneous.description: Find an ordered pair by elimination or substitution, then check it in both equations.

sections.title: Which terms can I cancel?
sections.label: Eliminate
sections.intro: An ordered pair must satisfy both equations. Adding two equalities can remove a letter when its coefficients are opposites.

blocks.html: Add for opposite coefficients. Subtract for equal coefficients.

figure.alt: Two distinct straight lines intersect at one marked point.
figure.caption: The point where the lines meet satisfies both equations.

blocks.prompt: Solve the simultaneous equations \(4x+y=59\) and \(7x-y=84\). Give an ordered pair \((x,y)\).
blocks.hint: Find one value first. Put it back in an original equation to find the other.
blocks.solution:
Add the two equations to remove y. The equal and opposite coefficients cancel.

The result is \(11x=143\). Solve for x, then use the first equation to find y.

The answer is \((13,7)\).

blocks.html: After finding one letter, substitute it to find the other.

blocks.prompt: Solve the simultaneous equations \(7x+y=31\) and \(4x-y=13\). Give an ordered pair \((x,y)\).
blocks.hint: Find one value first. Put it back in an original equation to find the other.
blocks.solution:
Add the two equations to remove y. The equal and opposite coefficients cancel.

The result is \(11x=44\). Solve for x, then use the first equation to find y.

The answer is \((4,3)\).

sections.title: When is substitution shorter?
sections.label: Substitute
sections.intro: If a letter is already alone, replace that letter in the other equation with its expression.

blocks.html: Use the whole expression when replacing it. Solve the remaining equation in one letter.

blocks.prompt: Solve \(y=5x-2\) and \(2x+y=12\) together. Give an ordered pair \((x,y)\).
blocks.hint: Find one value first. Put it back in an original equation to find the other.
blocks.solution:
Use the expression for \(y\) from the first equation in the second equation.

Collect the terms to get \(7x=14\). After dividing, substitute to find \(y\).

The answer is \((2,8)\).

blocks.html: Put the two values back in the same order as the requested pair.

blocks.prompt: Solve \(y=3x-11\) and \(5x+y=29\) together. Give an ordered pair \((x,y)\).
blocks.hint: Find one value first. Put it back in an original equation to find the other.
blocks.solution:
Use the expression for \(y\) from the first equation in the second equation.

Collect the terms to get \(8x=40\). After dividing, substitute to find \(y\).

The answer is \((5,4)\).

sections.title: How can I form two equations from the facts?
sections.label: Receipts
sections.intro: Define both unknowns with a unit. Each total gives a separate equation in the same two unknowns.

blocks.html: Arrange like terms in the same columns so you can see what cancels.

blocks.prompt: A receipt shows 9 large craft packs and one small pack cost £36. Another shows 3 large packs and one small pack cost £18. Find both prices. Give (large, small) in pounds.
blocks.hint: Find one value first. Put it back in an original equation to find the other.
blocks.solution:
Let \(x\) and \(y\) be the larger and smaller pack prices, in pounds. The two receipts give \(9x+y=36\) and \(3x+y=18\).

Subtract the second equation from the first. This leaves \(6x=18\). Use the first receipt to find the small pack price.

The answer is \((3,9)\).

blocks.html: Use asked price order when you give the final pair.

blocks.prompt: A receipt shows 10 large craft packs and one small pack cost £65. Another shows 6 large packs and one small pack cost £41. Find both prices. Give (large, small) in pounds.
blocks.hint: Find one value first. Put it back in an original equation to find the other.
blocks.solution:
Let \(x\) and \(y\) be the larger and smaller pack prices, in pounds. The two receipts give \(10x+y=65\) and \(6x+y=41\).

Subtract the second equation from the first. This leaves \(4x=24\). Use the first receipt to find the small pack price.

The answer is \((6,5)\).

sections.title: When can I use two factors?
sections.label: Factors
sections.intro: Make one side zero first. If the quadratic factors, a product of two factors is zero when at least one of them is zero.

blocks.prompt: Solve \(x^2+1x-20=0\). Give both roots.
blocks.hint: A product of zero means at least one factor is zero.
blocks.solution:
Factorise using two numbers whose product is the constant and whose sum is the middle coefficient.

The equation becomes \((x+5)(x-4)=0\). Set each factor equal to zero.

The answer is \(x=-5\ \text{or}\ x=4\).

Take both square roots. Then add 6 to each of the two answers.

The answer is \(x=-2\ \text{or}\ x=14\).

The answer is \(x=5\ \text{or}\ x=13\).

sections.title: What if the new subject appears twice?
sections.label: Repeated
sections.intro: Bring both terms containing the new subject to the same side. Factor out that letter before dividing.

blocks.html: Write the letter once as a factor outside a bracket.

figure.caption: Start from the given result and work back through the operations.

blocks.prompt: Make x the subject of \(s=kx-14x\), where \(k\ne 14\).
blocks.hint: Keep the terms involving x together, then factor out x.
blocks.solution:
Factor out the common x to obtain \(s=(k-14)x\).

Divide both sides by \(k-14\), which is non-zero.

The answer is \(x=\frac{s}{k-14}\).

blocks.html: If dividing by an expression, that expression must be non-zero.

sections.title: How do I undo a square root?
sections.label: Root
sections.intro: Isolate the root, then square both sides. A principal square root has a non-negative value.

blocks.html: Check the sign condition before squaring. Keep the rest of the radicand grouped.

blocks.prompt: Given \(r=6\sqrt{x+4}\) with \(r\ge0\), make x the subject.
blocks.hint: Undo the outside multiplication before squaring.
blocks.solution:
Divide by \(6\) and square both sides to undo the square root.

Subtract \(4\) to leave x by itself.

The answer is \(x=\frac{r^2}{36}-4\).

blocks.html: Do not square only part of a fraction.

blocks.prompt: Given \(r=9\sqrt{x+7}\) with \(r\ge0\), make x the subject.
blocks.hint: Undo the outside multiplication before squaring.

Divide by \(9\) and square both sides to undo the square root.

Subtract \(7\) to leave x by itself.

The answer is \(x=\frac{r^2}{81}-7\).

sections.title: Which square root is allowed after rearranging?
sections.label: Power
sections.intro: Once a squared subject is isolated, read the sign restriction. In a length formula the appropriate root is non-negative.

blocks.html: State the sign condition. Without one a real squared equation can have two signs.

blocks.prompt: Given \(q=6x^2+5\) and \(x\ge0\), rearrange the formula to give x in terms of q. For this check, enter the expression for \(x^2\).
blocks.hint: Isolate the square before taking the root.
blocks.solution:
Subtract \(5\) and divide by \(6\) to isolate the square.

The intermediate expression gives x squared. Then take the non-negative root because \(x\ge0\).

Take the non-negative root because \(x\ge0\). \(x=\sqrt{\frac{q-5}{6}}\).

The answer is \(x^2=\frac{q-5}{6}\).
